Paper Title: Fault Attacks on CCA-Secure Lattice KEMs
Authors: Peter Pessl, Lukas Prokop
Fault Model: Random bit flip, zeroing, instruction skip
Attack Objective: Plaintext-Checking Oracle (PCO) to key recovery
Countermeasure Proposed: Double re-encryption, randomized order, parity
Experimental Scale: Simulated sweeps + real EMFI on ARM Cortex-M4
Main Result: Demonstrated that faulting the message decoding or re-encryption equality comparison reduces CCA security to CPA, enabling full secret key recovery via chosen ciphertexts.
Main Limitation: Requires adaptive chosen-ciphertext queries; assumes attacker can observe rejection/acceptance oracle without system lockouts.
Relevance to Our Project: Directly studies FO re-encryption and decapsulation faults in Kyber.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Analysis of FO predicate failure and equality bypass.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Focuses on adversarial key recovery rather than radiation-induced autonomous execution; does not model lossy compression diffusion thresholds or spacecraft framing pipelines.

Paper Title: Fault-Enabled Chosen-Ciphertext Attacks on Kyber
Authors: Julius Hermelink, Peter Pessl, Thomas Poeppelmann
Attack Objective: Turn decapsulation into Plaintext Checking Oracle (PCO)
Countermeasure Proposed: Redundant checks, randomizing comparison order
Experimental Scale: Analytical + simulated key recovery queries (approx 1000-4000 queries)
Main Result: Bypassing the ciphertext comparison check allows chosen-ciphertext attacks to extract secret key coefficients using belief propagation.
Main Limitation: Requires crafted malformed ciphertexts fed repeatedly to the target; cannot be executed passively with legitimate traffic.
Relevance to Our Project: Explains why FO comparison is a primary target in Kyber decapsulation.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Theoretical analysis of FO bypass.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not evaluate behavior under honest/random single-event upsets where attacker is absent; does not examine intermediate butterfly diffusion.

Paper Title: Roulette: A Diverse Family of Feasible Fault Attacks on Masked Kyber
Authors: Jeroen Delvaux
Fault Model: Bit-flip, byte zeroing, random fault, instruction skip
Fault Location: CBD binomial sampling, INTT butterflies, message decoding
Attack Objective: Key recovery bypassing higher-order masking
Countermeasure Proposed: Combined masking + infective computation, dual execution
Experimental Scale: Simulated Monte Carlo + physical EMFI glitching
Main Result: Demonstrated that even first- and second-order masked Kyber implementations can be broken by relaxing fault precision to binomial sampling and INTT loops.
Main Limitation: Focuses on bypassing side-channel masking countermeasures; relies on repeated targeted injections.
Relevance to Our Project: Analyzes faults inside CBD sampling and polynomial arithmetic.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Identifies CBD sampling and NTT/INTT as sensitive regions.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Evaluates attack efficiency against masking rather than characterization of natural SEUs, error absorption thresholds, or protocol desynchronization.

Paper Title: Fiddling the Twiddle Constants: Fault Injection Analysis of the Number Theoretic Transform
Authors: Prasanna Ravi, Bolin Yang, Shivam Bhasin, Fan Zhang, Anupam Chattopadhyay
Attack Objective: Entropy reduction leading to key recovery and signature forgery
Countermeasure Proposed: Constant integrity checksums, redundant table storage
Experimental Scale: Extensive simulation on pqm4 + FPGA accelerator
Main Result: Zeroizing twiddle factors collapses polynomial multiplication entropy, reducing lattice security from 128+ bits to solvable linear algebra.
Main Limitation: Assumes permanent or persistent corruptions of static lookup tables, not transient computational upsets inside arithmetic pipelines.
Relevance to Our Project: Identifies NTT twiddle table as a high-value vulnerability target.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Study of NTT mathematical degradation under corrupt coefficients.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not model transient single-event butterfly flips or investigate why early butterfly perturbations are absorbed by rounding.

Paper Title: Side-Channel and Fault-Injection Attacks Over Lattice-Based Post-Quantum Schemes: Survey and New Results
Authors: Prasanna Ravi, Shivam Bhasin, Sujoy Sinha Roy, Anupam Chattopadhyay
Fault Model: Survey of multi-fault models (SEU, DFA, skip, safe-error)
Attack Objective: Comprehensive systematization of attacks and countermeasures
Countermeasure Proposed: Algorithmic sanity checks, verify-after-sign, double-exec
Experimental Scale: Survey covering 50+ papers and independent case studies
Main Result: Systematizes attack vectors across PQC candidates, establishing that polynomial arithmetic and control-flow checks represent 80%+ of published vulnerabilities.
Main Limitation: Broad survey; does not provide cross-implementation empirical sensitivity maps or formal verification of resilience hooks.
Relevance to Our Project: Authoritative state-of-the-art benchmark for PQC implementation attacks.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Taxonomy of fault targets across ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Survey leaves open the problem of fine-grained sensitivity maps and space-communication protocol impacts.

Paper Title: Fault Injection Attacks on the Comparison Step of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transform
Authors: Anirudh Jaiswal, Sayandeep Saha, Debdeep Mukhopadhyay
Fault Type: Transient bit flip in comparison flag/mask
Attack Objective: Chosen-ciphertext key recovery via biased oracle
Countermeasure Proposed: Infective comparison, hardware cryptographic boolean checkers
Experimental Scale: Simulated oracle attack with 1500 queries + laser validation
Main Result: Proved that multi-word ciphertext equality checks (Booleanisation) cannot be protected by simple branch-skipping mitigations if intermediate accumulator registers can be faulted.
Main Limitation: Requires an active adversary with physical laser access repeatedly injecting faults during decapsulation queries.
Relevance to Our Project: Deeply relevant to our FO bidirectional verification experiments.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Analysis of ct_memcmp and fail flag vulnerability.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not examine the case where ciphertext corruption is accidental (space radiation) and legitimate keys are unrecoverable regardless of flag inversion.

Paper Title: Differential Fault Attacks on Deterministic Lattice Signatures
Authors: Leon Groot Bruinderink, Peter Pessl
Fault Location: Secret key polynomial during signing or intermediate nonce y
Fault Timing: During signature generation before Fiat-Shamir hash
Attack Objective: Secret key recovery via differential signature pairs
Countermeasure Proposed: Randomized signing (hedged mode), double signing verification
Experimental Scale: Analytical proof + simulated key recovery in <50 faulty signatures
Main Result: Showed that deterministic Dilithium is vulnerable to DFA: a single fault in the nonce y or secret vector s yields a faulty/clean signature pair that exposes the private key via linear equations.
Main Limitation: Only applies to deterministic signing; neutralized if fresh physical randomness is used for every signature.
Relevance to Our Project: Core justification for why FIPS 204 mandates hedged/randomized signing by default.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Analysis of Dilithium signing pipeline vulnerability.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not address whether hedged Dilithium can still be compromised, nor does it quantify rejection loop hang/timeout probabilities.

Paper Title: Correction Fault Attacks on Randomized CRYSTALS-Dilithium
Authors: Fabian Krahmer, Peter Pessl, Robert Land, Tim Gueneysu
Fault Model: Random byte flip, Rowhammer bit flip
Attack Objective: Key recovery against randomized (hedged) Dilithium
Countermeasure Proposed: Strict norm verification before release, verify-after-sign
Experimental Scale: Simulated lattice reduction + Rowhammer proof-of-concept
Main Result: Overcomes Dilithium's randomized hedging defense by using public verification to 'correct' faulty signatures, creating a noisy linear system solvable by Integer Linear Programming.
Main Limitation: Requires several hundred faulty signatures and high compute time for lattice reduction (ILP / BKZ).
Relevance to Our Project: Proves that hedging alone is insufficient against fault attacks on Dilithium.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Exploration of Dilithium rejection and norm decomposition.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Focuses exclusively on cryptanalytic key extraction, not on execution availability, loop termination bounds, or communication link impacts.

Paper Title: Lattice-Based Signature Schemes and Their Sensitivity to Fault Attacks
Authors: Nina Bindel, Johannes Buchmann, Juliane Kraemer
Fault Location: Rejection sampling condition, secret key, commitment
Fault Timing: Signing rejection loops and norm checks
Attack Objective: Key extraction and signature forgery
Countermeasure Proposed: Algorithmic redundancy, norm bounding checks
Experimental Scale: Analytical vulnerability catalog
Main Result: First systematic sensitivity categorization of lattice signature components, identifying rejection sampling as the primary single point of failure.
Main Limitation: Pre-dates CRYSTALS-Dilithium and FIPS 204; lacked empirical campaign on production standard code.
Relevance to Our Project: Foundational conceptual origin of lattice signature fault sensitivity analysis.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Categorization of rejection sampling and norm checks.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Lacks concrete evaluation of FIPS 204 parameters, SHAKE-based hint bit generation, and modern vector instructions.

Paper Title: Hampering Fault Attacks Against Lattice-Based Signature Schemes - Countermeasures and Their Efficiency
Authors: Nina Bindel, Jens Hambitzer, Juliane Kraemer
Fault Type: Transient faults in arithmetic & control flow
Fault Location: Polynomial arithmetic, norm verification, signature encoding
Attack Objective: Mitigation of DFA and loop bypass
Countermeasure Proposed: Verify-after-sign, checksumming, loop counters, double-exec
Experimental Scale: Analytical performance modeling across multiple algorithms
Main Result: Evaluated trade-offs between temporal redundancy (100%+ overhead) and algorithmic assertions (10-30% overhead), showing assertions can catch specific DFA classes.
Main Limitation: Did not test against modern AVX2/NEON vector implementations or FIPS 204; relied on analytical overhead approximations rather than hardware measurements.
Relevance to Our Project: Directly motivates our RQ5 (Selective/Adaptive Resilience) and overhead trade-off metrics.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Trade-off analysis between full redundancy and selective assertions.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not connect detection mechanisms to autonomous spacecraft recovery, CCSDS packet framing, or cross-implementation portability.

Paper Title: Efficient Algorithm-Level Error Detection for Number-Theoretic Transform Used for Kyber Assessed on FPGAs and ARM
Authors: Mehran Mozaffari-Kermani, Reza Azarderakhsh, et al.
Fault Model: Bit flips, transient glitches in multipliers
Fault Timing: During NTT forward and inverse execution
Attack Objective: Error detection / fault tolerance
Countermeasure Proposed: Algebraic Invariant Checking (AIC), RESWO recomputation
Experimental Scale: Extensive FPGA synthesis (Xilinx Artix-7/Zynq) + ARM Cortex-A
Main Result: Achieved >99.9% fault coverage on NTT butterfly units with <25% hardware area overhead and <18% latency overhead using algebraic invariants.
Main Limitation: Focused specifically on the isolated NTT hardware accelerator; does not evaluate full end-to-end decapsulation, FO re-encryption, or protocol-level effects.
Relevance to Our Project: State-of-the-art in NTT fault detection mechanisms.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: NTT butterfly error detection and algebraic invariants.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not investigate the interaction between NTT error diffusion and ciphertext compression rounding, which our experiments revealed.

Paper Title: Error Detection Schemes Assessed on FPGA for Multipliers in Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanisms in Post-Quantum Cryptography
Authors: Amir Sarker, Mehran Mozaffari-Kermani, Reza Azarderakhsh
Venue: IEEE Trans. Emerging Topics in Computing (TETC)
Attack Objective: Reliable and fault-secure polynomial multiplication
Countermeasure Proposed: Recomputation with Negated/Swapped Operands (RENO/RESWO)
Experimental Scale: Comprehensive FPGA benchmarking across Xilinx UltraScale+
Main Result: Demonstrated that operand-encoding recomputation detects 99.97% of transient faults in Montgomery multipliers with modest DSP slice increase.
Main Limitation: Limited to hardware RTL primitives; overhead in software (pure C/assembly) would be substantially higher (>100% CPU cycles).
Relevance to Our Project: Provides concrete error detection schemes for polynomial multipliers.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Fault coverage metrics for modular reduction.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not address software-only implementations where hardware recomputation units are unavailable, such as space flight software running on standard CPUs.

Paper Title: Error-Detecting Number Theoretic Transform Architectures for Lattice-Based Cryptography
Authors: Reza Fritzmann, Georg Sigl et al.
Venue: IEEE Trans. Circuits and Systems I (TCAS-I)
Fault Location: Butterfly processing elements, twiddle ROM, dual-port RAM
Attack Objective: Fault detection and mitigation of DFA
Countermeasure Proposed: Dual-rail logic, spatial redundancy, parity checking
Experimental Scale: Synthesized on TSMC 28nm and Xilinx UltraScale
Main Result: Showed that parity-preserving NTT butterfly architectures detect single-bit transient faults with 32% area overhead, preventing twiddle zeroization attacks.
Main Limitation: ASIC/FPGA specific; cannot be applied directly to pure C software implementations on commercial space processors without custom silicon.
Relevance to Our Project: Relevant to understanding hardware-level fault manifestation in NTT engines.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Butterfly unit fault models.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Assumes custom ASIC hardware modifications; irrelevant to software-only deployment on legacy spacecraft flight computers.

Paper Title: CRYSTALS-Kyber: A CCA-Secure Module-Lattice-Based KEM
Authors: Joppe Bos, Leo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrede Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, John M. Schanck, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehle
Attack Objective: IND-CCA2 security proof and baseline design
Countermeasure Proposed: Fujisaki-Okamoto transform with implicit rejection
Experimental Scale: Extensive cryptanalytic benchmarks
Main Result: Established Kyber's mathematical design, M-LWE hardness, 7-layer NTT structure, Centered Binomial Distribution sampling, and FO CCA transform.
Main Limitation: Does not analyze physical fault attacks or hardware implementation vulnerabilities.
Relevance to Our Project: Foundational mathematical and algorithmic specification of our ML-KEM research target.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Core algorithmic structure of ML-KEM.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Lacks any fault-injection analysis, fault sensitivity taxonomy, or resilience mechanisms.

Paper Title: CRYSTALS-Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme
Authors: Leo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrede Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehle
Attack Objective: EUF-CMA security proof and signature design
Countermeasure Proposed: Fiat-Shamir with aborts, randomized nonces, norm bounding
Experimental Scale: Extensive cryptanalytic benchmarks
Main Result: Established Dilithium's design: Module-SIS/LWE security, 60-line signing loop, rejection sampling on infinity norms, HighBits/LowBits rounding, and hints.
Main Limitation: Does not analyze physical fault attacks or hardware implementation vulnerabilities.
Relevance to Our Project: Foundational mathematical and algorithmic specification of our ML-DSA research target.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Core algorithmic structure of ML-DSA.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Lacks fault-injection analysis, rejection loop hang characterization, or resilience mechanisms.

Paper Title: Formally Verified Implementations of ML-KEM in mlkem-native
Authors: Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance (PQCA) / AWS Automated Reasoning Group
Fault Location: Full C codebase and AArch64/x86_64 assembly
Attack Objective: Prove memory safety, type safety, functional correctness, constant-time
Countermeasure Proposed: Formal function contracts, loop invariants, proof annotations
Experimental Scale: Full proof coverage of all ML-KEM parameter sets (512, 768, 1024)
Main Result: Proved mathematically that mlkem-native is free of buffer overflows, undefined behavior, and secret-dependent timing channels under standard C semantics.
Main Limitation: Assumes fault-free hardware execution semantics; CBMC proofs do NOT hold when hardware bit-flips or instruction skips occur.
Relevance to Our Project: Our exact Path B source-level implementation under test (commit fc269bc2d106).
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Identical codebase used for our internal fault injection hooks.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: The existing CBMC verification guarantees zero bugs under normal execution, making it the ideal baseline to isolate the pure effect of injected faults.

Paper Title: High-Assurance Post-Quantum Cryptography: Jasmin and EasyCrypt Implementations of Kyber
Authors: Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Benjamin Gregoire, Peter Schwabe, Pierre-Yves Strub et al.
Attack Objective: Prove functional correctness, constant-time, and cryptographic IND-CCA security
Countermeasure Proposed: End-to-end verified compilation, machine-checked proofs
Experimental Scale: Complete verification of AVX2 optimized Kyber implementation
Main Result: Delivered the first machine-checked proof linking high-level IND-CCA cryptographic security down to assembly code via EasyCrypt and Jasmin.
Main Limitation: Assumes fault-free hardware execution; does not model or verify behavior under transient hardware faults or single-event upsets.
Relevance to Our Project: Demonstrates the gold standard in formal verification of cryptographic software.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Mathematical formalization of Kyber operations.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Does not extend formal proofs to fault-tolerance properties or evaluate resilience under memory/arithmetic upsets.

Paper Title: VerFI: A Verification Tool for Fault Injection Resistance of Cryptographic Hardware
Authors: Victor Arribas, Felix Wegener, Amir Moradi
Attack Objective: Automated formal verification of hardware countermeasure coverage
Countermeasure Proposed: Automated evaluation of redundancy and error detection
Experimental Scale: Benchmarked on dozens of cryptographic hardware netlists
Main Result: Automated the evaluation of fault injection resistance for hardware implementations, identifying sneak paths and glitch-propagation vulnerabilities.
Main Limitation: Restricted to hardware netlists (ASIC/FPGA); cannot analyze C software implementations or complex lattice polynomial arithmetic.
Relevance to Our Project: Highlights the state-of-the-art methodology for systematic fault coverage verification.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Methodology for automated fault injection sweeps.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Tooling cannot ingest C code, pointer structures, or floating/fixed-point polynomial rings like R_q.

Paper Title: FIVER: Formal Verification of Countermeasures Against Fault Injection Attacks
Authors: Jan Richter-Brockmann, Pascal Sasdrich, Tim Gueneysu
Attack Objective: Exhaustive formal verification of fault detection coverage without simulation
Countermeasure Proposed: BDD-based countermeasure validation
Experimental Scale: Evaluated against standard authenticated ciphers and block ciphers
Main Result: Eliminated the need for Monte Carlo fault simulation by formally proving whether an RTL circuit detects 100% of faults in a specified fault model using BDDs.
Main Limitation: Limited to symmetric primitives with small state spaces; intractable for 256-degree polynomials with 12-to-23-bit moduli like ML-KEM/ML-DSA.
Relevance to Our Project: Demonstrates what formal fault verification looks like when mathematically rigorous.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Formal classification of fault outcomes.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Explains why symbolic execution of lattice PQC requires different abstractions than bit-level BDDs.

Paper Title: Mitigating Single Event Effects, Hardware and Software Approaches
Authors: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
Fault Model: Single Event Effects (SEU, SET, SEFI, SEL, MBU)
Fault Location: SRAM, DRAM, Flash, CPU registers, logic gates
Attack Objective: System dependability, fault tolerance, mission survival
Countermeasure Proposed: TMR, EDAC, watchdog timers, software checkpointing, memory scrubbing
Experimental Scale: Decades of NASA spaceflight mission data and radiation test data
Main Result: Authoritative aerospace engineering guide on how ionizing radiation induces transient bit-flips (SEUs) and control-flow disruptions (SEFIs), and how to mitigate them in flight software.
Main Limitation: General spacecraft engineering handbook; does not mention post-quantum cryptography or lattice-based mathematical structures.
Relevance to Our Project: Primary authoritative standard defining realistic space radiation fault models.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Defines SEU, SET, and SEFI fault models.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Highlights the critical research gap: existing space standards have never analyzed the unique algorithmic vulnerabilities of lattice PQC.

Paper Title: End-to-End Quantum-Safe Security for Satellite Data Links (E2EQSS)
Authors: European Space Agency (ESA) / E2EQSS Consortium
Fault Model: Packet loss, channel noise, long latency (communication faults)
Fault Type: Bit errors in RF link, dropped CCSDS frames
Attack Objective: Evaluate feasibility of PQC key exchange and signatures over CCSDS/SDLS links
Countermeasure Proposed: Hybrid key exchange (ECDH + ML-KEM), optimized SDLS framing
Experimental Scale: Simulated LEO and GEO satellite downlinks with variable bit error rates
Main Result: Demonstrated that ML-KEM and ML-DSA can be integrated into CCSDS Space Data Link Security (SDLS) frames, but large signature/key sizes increase packet fragmentation and handshake latency.
Main Limitation: Focused exclusively on communication channel overhead and packet size constraints; did NOT study on-board processor fault injection, radiation upsets, or algorithmic resilience.
Relevance to Our Project: Directly establishes the operational context of PQC deployment in satellite data links.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Integration of PQC with CCSDS/SDLS communication frames.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Proves that while communication-layer PQC integration is studied, on-board computational fault resilience under radiation remains completely unaddressed.

Paper Title: Space Product Assurance: Radiation Hardness Assurance - EEE Components
Authors: European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS)
Fault Model: Heavy ions, protons, electrons, cosmic rays
Fault Location: Semiconductor silicon, memory cells, logic gates
Physical/Simulated: Heavy ion accelerator beam testing & radiation modeling
Attack Objective: Space qualification of electronic components
Countermeasure Proposed: Radiation shielding, rad-hard components, redundancy
Experimental Scale: Decades of ESA mission qualifications
Main Result: Standardizes testing protocols for measuring SEE cross-sections and LET thresholds in space electronics, distinguishing single-bit upsets from multi-bit upsets and destructive latchups.
Main Limitation: Physical electronics standard; does not address software algorithms, cryptography, or mathematical error propagation.
Relevance to Our Project: Provides the authoritative physical grounding for why software fault injection models must reflect physical SEE mechanisms.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Distinction between physical SEEs and abstract software mutations.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Underlines that software-level bit-flip campaigns are simulations of physical upsets and must be validated against physical cross-section realities.

Paper Title: Fault Analysis of Cryptographic Implementations: From Classical to Post-Quantum Schemes
Authors: Sikhar Patranabis, Debdeep Mukhopadhyay
Fault Model: Differential Fault Analysis, Fault Sensitivity Analysis, Safe-Error
Fault Type: Transient bit-flip, byte fault, instruction skip, clock glitch
Attack Objective: Comprehensive survey of fault attack techniques across cryptographic paradigms
Countermeasure Proposed: Infective computation, algorithmic checksums, parity, dual execution
Experimental Scale: Survey covering 150+ research papers
Main Result: Traced the evolution of fault attacks from symmetric/classical schemes to lattice cryptography, concluding that lattice schemes have unique vulnerabilities in Gaussian/binomial sampling and modular polynomial reduction.
Main Limitation: Broad survey; did not provide quantitative empirical comparative sensitivity maps across standard FIPS implementations.
Relevance to Our Project: Excellent academic reference establishing the state of fault analysis methodologies.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Taxonomy of fault models across cryptographic schemes.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Lacks concrete evaluation of FIPS 203/204 standard implementations and aerospace communication protocols.

Paper Title: Security Evaluation of Post-Quantum Cryptography in Satellite Networks
Authors: Christian Geissler, Daniel Loebenberger, et al.
Attack Objective: Evaluate bandwidth and latency impact of PQC in CubeSats
Countermeasure Proposed: Optimized fragmentation, compression of public keys
Experimental Scale: Emulated CubeSat ground passes with 9.6 kbps to 1 Mbps links
Main Result: Showed that ML-KEM-768 is practical for LEO CubeSat links (<50ms overhead), but ML-DSA-65 signatures significantly increase transmission time due to large signature sizes.
Main Limitation: Purely a network performance evaluation; did not investigate fault injection, processor radiation effects, or algorithmic dependability.
Relevance to Our Project: Validates the practical relevance of ML-KEM and ML-DSA in real satellite communication links.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Assessment of ML-KEM and ML-DSA in satellite communication passes.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Directly highlights that previous space PQC literature has ignored processor-level fault resilience.

Paper Title: Rowhammer-Assisted Fault Attacks on Post-Quantum Lattice Cryptography
Authors: Zhi Zhang, Yueqiang Cheng et al.
Fault Location: Page tables, polynomial buffers, secret key storage in DRAM
Attack Objective: Privilege escalation and cryptographic key extraction
Countermeasure Proposed: ECC DRAM, memory isolation, B-Tree refreshing
Experimental Scale: Physical testbeds on modern Intel/AMD platforms
Main Result: Demonstrated that software attackers without physical physical laboratory access can use Rowhammer to flip bits in DRAM holding Kyber secret keys or Dilithium signing buffers to extract private keys.
Main Limitation: Requires colocated malicious processes on the same physical host; not applicable to isolated embedded space processors.
Relevance to Our Project: Demonstrates that software-level bit-flips can accurately mirror real physical bit-flips in memory.
Exact Overlap with Our Current Work: Memory bit-flip model on lattice data structures.
Potential Gap Relative to Our Project: Space systems do not suffer from multi-tenant Rowhammer exploits, but experience identical physical DRAM bit flips from cosmic ray heavy ions.
